entities.name: Ghana Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Ghana Empire (c. 300-1235 CE), the first of the great West African Sahelian empires (preceding Mali and Songhai), controlled the trans-Saharan trade routes between North Africa and sub-Saharan West Africa from its capital Koumbi Saleh (in modern Mauritania), taxing the gold and salt caravans that made it one of the ancient world's wealthiest states. Arab geographer al-Bakri's 1068 CE description of Ghana's royal court — its gold-adorned king, its silent court protocol, its enormous army — provides the most detailed contemporary account of a sub-Saharan African polity before the Islamic period.

Ghana's wealth came from its strategic position between the gold fields of Bambuk and Bure (in modern Guinea) and the Saharan salt mines of Taghaza: Ghana imposed a tax of one gold dinar on every load of salt entering and two dinars on every load leaving; gold was similarly taxed. By controlling this bottleneck, Ghana's kings accumulated legendary wealth — Arab sources describe the king's court as having 1,000 horses, each sleeping on a carpet with three servants, their halters decorated with gold. The empire's army at its peak was reportedly 200,000 strong.

Ghana's decline came from multiple directions: the Almoravid Berber movement's 1076 CE sack of Koumbi Saleh disrupted trade routes; prolonged drought in the Sahel reduced agricultural productivity; and the rising Mali Empire under Sundiata Keita defeated Ghana definitively in 1235 CE. Though the Ghana Empire as a political entity ended, it established the template of Sahelian empire — trans-Saharan trade control, sophisticated Islamic-African court culture — that the Mali and Songhai Empires would replicate and expand.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Ghana Empire — controlling the trans-Saharan gold-salt trade for nearly a millennium, generating legendary wealth documented by Arab geographers, and establishing the Sahelian empire template that Mali and Songhai would use — was Africa's first documented great empire and the foundation of West Africa's medieval golden age.
